Read IN FULL: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-marcel-a-n-navarro-Dev/646bc8ac-afb6-41b4-8d24-dcbaf28144cd/scratchpad/turns_chunk06.txt

This file contains every user turn Marcel Navarro typed across ~46 Claude Code sessions while working as FED Lead on the Zimmermann PWA Kit (a Salesforce PWA Kit / React / Chakra codebase). Sessions are separated by `====` lines with a `### [tag] [date] Title — N user turns` header. Turns are marked `--- turn N ---`.

READ THE WHOLE FILE. It is large (~451,000 tokens), so read it in sequential slices using Read with offset/limit. Maintain a running findings list as you go and DISCARD raw text after each slice — never try to hold the whole file in context.

We are designing personal workflow skills for Marcel. The transcripts are the evidence for WHY those skills are needed. Extract these six things:

**1. RECURRING CORRECTIONS — the highest priority.**
Places where Marcel had to re-state an established way of working that had been ignored or got wrong. He has said he had to "stress again and again" the set approach. Find those. For each, give: verbatim quote (trimmed to the relevant sentences), the session title, turn number, and tag it with the area:
`overriding` | `tokens` | `components` | `atomic-design` (atoms/molecules/organisms) | `css-structure` | `css-strategy` | `tests` | `stories` | `a11y` | `typescript` | `contentful` | `scope` | `git/branching` | `other`
Count how many DISTINCT times each area comes up. That count is the single most important output.

**2. DESIGN CONFORMANCE.**
Where he had to check or re-check that a build matched the Figma design — variants, states, tokens, viewports, spacing. Quote the checks he actually performs and what he looks for.

**3. FRUSTRATION / RE-WORK SIGNALS.**
Turns containing corrections: "again", "I said", "no —", "that's not", "you missed", "why did you", "revert", "you were supposed to", "as I mentioned". These mark where the workflow broke down. Quote and categorise.

**4. WHAT WORKED.**
Successes. Especially any use of a closed-loop / multi-agent / orchestrator-builder-tester-scorer workflow. Quote how he set it up and what he said about the result. Also note any prompt pattern he reused because it worked.

**5. HIS PROMPT FORMULAS.**
Recurring phrasings and structures he types — the shape of his asks. We want to encode his voice and method into skills, so capture the actual language, not a paraphrase.

**6. REVIEW-MODE BEHAVIOUR.**
He is also senior dev / reviewer. Where he reviews others' PRs or code, capture: what he checks, in what order, what he rejects, and how he phrases feedback.

OUTPUT: a structured report with these six sections. Lead section 1 with a frequency table of areas. Use verbatim quotes throughout — quotes are the deliverable, not summaries. Be concrete. If a section has nothing, say so explicitly.

4	
5	
6	
7	PR REVIEW AS A CLOSED LOOP
8	
9	
10	
11	The shape is four stages. What makes it work is that you hold the ground truth and the adjudication, and delegate only the reading. Reviewers are cheap and fallible; measurements are expensive and authoritative. Keep those on opposite sides of the line.
12	
13	
14	
15	
16	
17	STAGE 0 — ESTABLISH GROUND TRUTH YOURSELF
18	
19	
20	
21	Before spinning up a single agent, do four things. Every later stage depends on this.
22	
23	
24	
25	Check out the PR branch and record the frame: base SHA, head SHA, files changed, plus/minus lines. You will refer back to this constantly when a reviewer claims something changed that did not.
26	
27	
28	
29	Get the ticket verbatim. Not your summary, not the PR description's paraphrase — the actual acceptance criteria as written. Every scope argument later gets decided against those words, and handing reviewers your compression of it pre-decides the scope question for them. A reviewer given a wrong premise wastes an entire pass.
30	
31	
32	
33	Run every deterministic gate and write down the raw numbers. Typecheck, tests, lint, build, any repo-specific audit script. Then run them again on the base SHA. This is the PR-specific step people skip: without a baseline you cannot distinguish a failure the PR introduced from one it inherited, and you will burn reviewer budget on both.
34	
35	
36	
37	Read the repo's own convention docs — CONTRIBUTING, AGENTS.md, .claude/rules/, whatever exists. These are the rubric. A reviewer applying general best practice instead of house rules generates noise that reads like signal.
38	
39	
40	
41	Three traps to check before trusting any gate number:
42	
43	
44	
45	1. Non-zero at a healthy baseline. Lint exits 1 with pre-existing errors; an audit script exits 1 with known violations. Diff the counts, ignore the exit code. Treating non-zero as failure means nothing ever passes.
46	
47	
48	
49	2. Passes having run nothing. Vitest's passWithNoTests, a path filter matching zero files, a --grep matching no tests. Assert on the reported item count, never the exit code.
50	
51	
52	
53	3. Stderr noise on a passing run. Parser warnings, deprecation notices. Note them explicitly so reviewers do not flag them as findings.
54	
55	
56	
57	
58	
59	STAGE 1 — FAN OUT
60	
61	
62	
63	Launch three or four reviewers in parallel, fresh contexts, not forks. A fork inherits your assumptions about what "done" looks like, which is exactly what you want tested.
64	
65	
66	
67	Give each: the diff, the ticket verbatim, and your measured gate numbers. Then forbid them from re-running the gates. You already measured; their budget should go entirely on what gates cannot see.
68	
69	
70	
71	Briefs should be distinct but overlapping — that overlap is the mechanism. Two agents converging independently is your confidence signal; two agents disagreeing is where you learn something.
72	
73	
74	
75	Angles that work, adapted to what the diff touches:
76	
77	
78	
79	- Correctness and regression. Does it do what the ticket says? What breaks that the diff does not obviously touch? Trace call sites of anything modified.
80	
81	- Conventions and structure. Against the repo's own docs. Naming, layering, imports, required tests and stories, ownership and tier rules.
82	
83	- Contract fidelity. If the PR ports, wraps, overrides or extends something, diff against the original and confirm every delta is deliberate. Prop surfaces, public APIs, error behaviour.
84	
85	- Failure modes. Error handling, silent failures, fallbacks that mask bugs, security-sensitive paths — logged credentials, unsanitised HTML, injection.
86	
87	
88	
89	Constraints to impose on every reviewer. These are the parts that produce findings rather than summaries. Phrase them how you like, but keep all of them:
90	
91	
92	
93	- Falsify, do not confirm. Try to break each claim the PR makes about itself.
94	
95	- Cite file:line, and label every finding CONFIRMED or PLAUSIBLE — reproduced versus reasoned-but-unproven. That distinction is what lets you triage fast later.
96	
97	- Severity: BLOCKER, DEFECT, or NOTE.
98	
99	- When a count moves, prove which items moved, not just how many. A total going 19 to 14 looks like proof and is not — it is equally consistent with a deleted item or a mutated value. Where the set is small enough, settle identity by enumerating it.
100	
101	- For any check whose pass you are relying on, try to make it pass wrongly. Inject a decoy that should fail and confirm it does. A check never made to fail has not been shown capable of failing.
102	
103	- Any "X exists nowhere" claim must state its search scope in the same sentence. Scope is part of the finding, not context around it.
104	
105	- Separate what the author changed from what was already there. Pre-existing issues are NOTEs unless the PR's own premise makes them defects.
106	
107	- Mandatory closing section: "What I could not verify." Name what you could not reach and why. If you think the space is covered, show the search. An empty section with no reasoning is a failed brief.
108	
109	
110	
111	
112	
113	STAGE 2 — ADJUDICATE, AND THIS IS YOURS ALONE
114	
115	
116	
117	This is where the loop earns its cost. Do not delegate it.
118	
119	
120	
121	Where reviewers agree, accept it. Independent convergence is the strongest signal you have.
122	
123	
124	
125	Where they disagree, go to source yourself. Do not average them, and do not take the more confident one — confidence and correctness are not correlated in agent output. Record which you checked and what settled it.
126	
127	
128	
129	Where a reviewer's conclusion is broader than its search supports, downgrade it. This is the single most common failure mode: the search is correct, the claim overreaches. "This exists nowhere" almost always means "nowhere I looked."
130	
131	
132	
133	Expect roughly a third of findings to be confidently wrong. A reviewer refuting its own sub-finding is the system working, not budget wasted.
134	
135	
136	
137	Treat inherited attributions as claims, not measurements. If a reviewer tells you "this line is unchanged from upstream," that is a claim it may have inherited from the PR's own comments. Verify before repeating it — passing one through as fact is an easy way to launder an error into your own report.
138	
139	
140	
141	Scope in both directions. Flag under-delivery and over-delivery against the ticket. Anything beyond what was asked gets surfaced for a human ruling — do not silently accept it, and do not demand its removal either.
142	
143	
144	
145	And name one premise everyone agreed on, then make someone attack it. Shared assumptions are invisible precisely because they are shared. This is the highest-yield single move in the whole workflow.
146	
147	
148	
149

158

162	
163	3. What nobody verified. The union of the reviewers' gaps, minus anything you closed. State plainly what a human still has to check by hand or in a browser. This section is the honest one, and it is what stops a clean result reading as proof.
164	
165	4. Your adjudications. Every disagreement and what settled it.
166	
167	
168	
169	Nothing gets posted to the PR unless you decide to post it.
170	
171	
172	
173	
174	
175	IF YOU TRIM IT, KEEP THESE FOUR
176	
177	
178	
179	Everything above is scaffolding around four instructions that do most of the work:
180	
181	
182	
183	Mandatory "what I could not verify." Reviewers naturally report what they checked, which reads as completeness. Forcing an explicit gap list surfaces the thing nobody looked at.
184	
185	
186	
187	Prove which items moved, not how many. Each level of rigour — moved number, then conserved total, then identity by exhaustion — closes a hole the previous one leaves open.
188	
189	
190	
191	State your search scope in the same sentence. Turns an overreaching conclusion back into an accurate one.
192	
193	
194	
195	Do not ratify the chain. Make the shared premise explicit and attack it.

## 4. WHAT WORKED

### The closed-loop multi-agent PR review — his own written methodology

`PR #61 review access`, 2026-08-27, **turn 3**. He opened the session by pasting a complete, self-authored workflow spec. This is the most valuable artefact in the chunk. Verbatim, condensed to the load-bearing lines:

> "for this PR review, here's how we'll run it: **PR REVIEW AS A CLOSED LOOP**
> The shape is four stages. What makes it work is that **you hold the ground truth and the adjudication, and delegate only the reading. Reviewers are cheap and fallible; measurements are expensive and authoritative. Keep those on opposite sides of the line.**
>
> **STAGE 0 — ESTABLISH GROUND TRUTH YOURSELF.** …Check out the PR branch and record the frame: base SHA, head SHA, files changed, plus/minus lines. …**Get the ticket verbatim. Not your summary, not the PR description's paraphrase** — the actual acceptance criteria as written. …**Run every deterministic gate and write down the raw numbers. …Then run them again on the base SHA.** …Read the repo's own convention docs — CONTRIBUTING, AGENTS.md, .claude/rules/ … **These are the rubric.**
> Three traps: 1. **Non-zero at a healthy baseline** … 2. **Passes having run nothing.** Vitest's passWithNoTests, a path filter matching zero files, a --grep matching no tests. **Assert on the reported item count, never the exit code.** 3. **Stderr noise on a passing run.**
>
> **STAGE 1 — FAN OUT.** Launch three or four reviewers in parallel, **fresh contexts, not forks. A fork inherits your assumptions about what \"done\" looks like, which is exactly what you want tested.** …Give each: the diff, the ticket verbatim, and your measured gate numbers. **Then forbid them from re-running the gates.** …**Briefs should be distinct but overlapping — that overlap is the mechanism. Two agents converging independently is your confidence signal; two agents disagreeing is where you learn something.**
> Angles: **Correctness and regression** … **Conventions and structure. Against the repo's own docs. Naming, layering, imports, required tests and stories, ownership and tier rules.** … **Contract fidelity** … **Failure modes.**
> Constraints on every reviewer: **Falsify, do not confirm.** … **Cite file:line, and label every finding CONFIRMED or PLAUSIBLE.** … **Severity: BLOCKER, DEFECT, or NOTE.** … **When a count moves, prove which items moved, not just how many.** … **For any check whose pass you are relying on, try to make it pass wrongly. Inject a decoy that should fail and confirm it does. A check never made to fail has not been shown capable of failing.** … **Any \"X exists nowhere\" claim must state its search scope in the same sentence.** … **Separate what the author changed from what was already there.** … **Mandatory closing section: \"What I could not verify.\"** …
>
> **STAGE 2 — ADJUDICATE, AND THIS IS YOURS ALONE.** …**Where they disagree, go to source yourself. Do not average them, and do not take the more confident one — confidence and correctness are not correlated in agent output.** …**Where a reviewer's conclusion is broader than its search supports, downgrade it. This is the single most common failure mode.** …**Expect roughly a third of findings to be confidently wrong.** …**Treat inherited attributions as claims, not measurements.** …**Scope in both directions. Flag under-delivery and over-delivery against the ticket.** …**And name one premise everyone agreed on, then make someone attack it. …This is the highest-yield single move in the whole workflow.**
>
> **STAGE 3 — WHAT YOU PRODUCE.** 1. **Gate table.** 2. **Findings, ranked, BLOCKERs first.** 3. **What nobody verified.** …**This section is the honest one, and it is what stops a clean result reading as proof.** 4. **Your adjudications.** …**Nothing gets posted to the PR unless you decide to post it.**
>
> **IF YOU TRIM IT, KEEP THESE FOUR:** Mandatory \"what I could not verify.\" / Prove which items moved, not how many. / State your search scope in the same sentence. / **Do not ratify the chain.**"

## 6. REVIEW-MODE BEHAVIOUR

### What he checks, in order

From the closed-loop spec (`PR #61`, turn 3) and the playbook (`Ready to work` 08-19, turn 39), his review order is:

1. **Frame the diff before reading it** — "record the frame: base SHA, head SHA, files changed, plus/minus lines."
2. **Ticket verbatim, never a paraphrase** — "Get the ticket verbatim. Not your summary, not the PR description's paraphrase — the actual acceptance criteria as written. Every scope argument later gets decided against those words."
3. **Deterministic gates, plus the same gates on base SHA** — "without a baseline you cannot distinguish a failure the PR introduced from one it inherited."
4. **House rules as the rubric** — "Read the repo's own convention docs — CONTRIBUTING, AGENTS.md, .claude/rules/… These are the rubric. A reviewer applying general best practice instead of house rules generates noise that reads like signal."
